title: The gulf of time
hookLine: look at the vast gulf of time behind you and ahead (Meditations 4.50)

cards: On a clear night, away from the streetlights, look up. Some of that light left its star centuries ago, long before anyone alive today was born. You're looking backward in time.
Plenty of people feel two things at once out there: very small, and strangely calm.
Marcus Aurelius had no telescope, but near the end of his fourth book he stands at the edge of the same view, and asks what it does to the length of one life.

teach.h: THINK OF THOSE WHO CLUNG TO LIFE.
teach.b: He starts with what he calls an unphilosophical but still useful aid against the fear of death: think of the people who clung hard to life. What did they gain over those who died young?
He names a few Romans who lived long and buried many others, and then were buried themselves. The gap between a short life and a long one, he says, is small. Then the view opens.

teach.h: THE GULF BEHIND, THE GULF AHEAD.
teach.b: Look at the vast gulf of time behind you, he writes, and the other boundless stretch ahead.
In that infinity, what's the difference between someone who lives three days and someone who lives three generations?
He seems to be playing on old Homer here: Nestor, the wise old king who outlived two generations of men and ruled among the third. Against the gulf, Nestor and an infant are almost the same size.
Some people find that view frightening. The French writer Blaise Pascal, many centuries later, wrote, in Trotter's 1910 translation: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me."
Marcus finds something else in it: relief.

If a life is a flicker in that dark either way, its length is not the thing to fight over. What matters is what you do inside your flicker. Both reactions are honest, and you may feel both on the same night.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take the view of Meditations 4.50 outdoors, looking at the night sky and measuring a worry against the vastness of time.

o: a Greek astronomer who first mapped the night sky
Homer's old king, long-lived yet tiny beside endless time
a Roman emperor who ruled long and was soon forgotten

games.q: the gulf of time — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus calls this a deep philosophical proof
he calls it unphilosophical, but still useful.
Marcus asks what separates three days from three generations
against the gulf of time, he says, very little.
Pascal and Marcus felt the same about the infinite
Pascal wrote that its silence frightened him; Marcus found relief.

games.q: you're up at 2am, sure that a mistake at work will define your whole life. what does Marcus reach for in 4.50?
o: make a detailed plan to fix your reputation.
look at the gulf of time behind and ahead.
decide you need to live longer to make up for it.
games.why: Marcus measures a life against the boundless time on either side: against it, the mistake, and even the life, are small.

practice: Look up at the sky if it's night, or picture it if you can't. Feel the time behind you, centuries and then more with no floor, and the time ahead, just as open, and find yourself in it: one breath, one small light.
Notice what comes, smallness or calm or both.

wordCard.voice: Nestor, the wise old king Marcus names, who outlived two generations and still measures almost the same against the gulf of time. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'age, eternity, a lifetime': the root of our word eon, and the vast time Marcus looks into.

carryVoice: Your line: almost the same size. What counts is what you do inside your flicker. Rest easy tonight.

sources.q: The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me.
